title: Counter-Positioning
hook: A folded clinic chair can threaten an office that cannot copy the price without wounding itself.
counterintuition: The old leader faces the opposite of easy imitation: copying the entrant means wounding the model that still pays the bills.
tryThisNow: Write the incumbent sentence: we cannot copy this because it would damage __. If the blank stays empty, the entrant is different, not counter-positioned.
keyTakeaway: Counter-positioning works when a newcomer uses a superior model that incumbents hesitate to copy because imitation would injure their existing economics.

breakdown.fastRead:
The folding dental chair clicks open under a warehouse light. Sophie places an employer subscription contract beside a clinic price sheet. Her mobile route is cheaper for routine visits because employers buy blocks of cleanings. A traditional office could copy the price, but the copy would cut into the visits that keep its chairs full.

Counter-positioning is not the same as disruption. The newcomer needs a better model, and the old leader needs a reason to flinch. If the incumbent can copy without hurting itself, the barrier is thin.
breakdown.deepRead:
Sophie marks the revenue line a traditional dental office would have to wound to match her offer. The office already earns from individual visits, insurance billing, and chair utilization. A subscription route to employers may fit her mobile clinic, but it forces the office to teach customers a lower, flatter way to buy routine care. The model is not just cheaper. It is awkward for the incumbent to imitate.

That is the mechanism: superior business model plus anticipated damage.

The Scylla and Charybdis image is useful because the incumbent is trapped between painful options. Copy the entrant and injure the old model. Ignore the entrant and let a new model grow. The incumbent may see the move clearly and still delay because both choices hurt.

Julien sees the same pattern in used cameras. He tags one body as rental-only, then puts the new-equipment margin sheet beside the deposit receipt. A retail camera shop can rent gear, but every successful rental may replace a sale the shop was built to protect.

A counter-positioned entrant does not win by being fashionable. It wins by making the old leader pay a price for copying.

That is why the entrant has to name the wound. Lower price, new channel, or cleaner software does not matter unless it forces the incumbent to damage something it still depends on.
breakdown.fullRead:
Anya stands over an hourly invoice with a flat-fee filing page open on the next screen. Her legal forms platform serves uncontested tenant filings. The incumbent law firm can build the same workflow. The hard part is what the workflow teaches clients: a routine filing does not need a partner clock running in six-minute slices.

This is the sharp test. Ask what the incumbent would have to make less valuable, less expensive, or less central in order to copy the entrant. The answer might be a fee structure, a dealer relationship, a retail shelf, a service habit, or a premium bundle. If no old profit line gets threatened, the entrant may still be good. It is not protected by counter-positioning.

The temptation is to call every new model counter-positioned. Online instead of physical. Subscription instead of purchase. Flat fee instead of hourly. Rental instead of retail. Those labels are not enough. The model has to be better for the chosen customer, and the incumbent has to face real damage from imitation. A weak entrant is just novel. A strong entrant turns the old leader's strengths into hesitation.

What would the incumbent have to betray?

Chidi answers with returned chair tags pinned under a new-stock price list. His refurbisher offers buy-back credits for modular furniture. A new-furniture store could imitate the credit, but each returned chair would teach customers that yesterday's product still has value outside the full-price shelf. The store would be funding a habit that competes with its own premium inventory.

There are limits. An incumbent might copy faster than expected if the old business is already collapsing or if the entrant's model does not touch a serious profit pool. A company with flexible channels, patient owners, and little attachment to the current model may absorb the pain. Counter-positioning is strongest when the old model is still profitable enough to defend.

Marco shows the barrier from another angle. In a venue office, a no-commission booking screen sits beside an agency commission ledger. Artists love the new payout. Agencies can see why. But copying it means explaining to staff and partners why the old fee column should shrink. The entrant's advantage is not moral purity. It is the incumbent's reluctance to injure its own ledger.

The question is never just, is the new model better? The second question carries the power: better for the entrant, painful for the incumbent. When both are true, hesitation becomes the newcomer's shield.

Use the incumbent sentence before you celebrate the entrant. We cannot copy this because it would damage our dealer channel. We cannot match this fee because it would shrink the work that trains junior staff. We cannot rent this product because it would teach customers not to buy the full-price version. If the sentence sounds empty, the new model may still be useful, but the counter-positioning claim is weak. The protection lives in the incumbent self-harm, not in the entrant novelty.

examples.title: Sophie marks the wounded clinic line

planSpec.domain: mobile dental clinic selling subscription visits to employers
planSpec.audience: founder comparing a subscription route against legacy fee-for-service offices
planSpec.stakes: incumbent clinics could copy the subscription but would undercut their appointment book
planSpec.requiredBeat: Sophie places the employer contract beside the clinic price sheet and marks the revenue line a traditional office would have to wound to match her offer.

examples.scenario: The folding dental chair clicks open under a fluorescent warehouse light while Sophie sets an employer contract beside a clinic price sheet. Her route calendar can fill Tuesday mornings with subscription cleanings. The old office across town could match the price only by cutting its single-visit revenue. Her pen rests on the contract while she must decide whether that wounded revenue line is the barrier or just a sales story.
examples.whatToDo: Mark the incumbent revenue line that would shrink if it copied the subscription. Build the offer only where the mobile model improves value and makes the office harm its own economics.
examples.whyItMatters: Counter-positioning needs both halves. The entrant model must work better for the customer, and imitation must damage the incumbent business enough to slow copying.

examples.title: Julien tags the rental camera

planSpec.domain: used-camera rental service competing with retail camera shops
planSpec.audience: reader deciding whether a rental model creates an incumbent copying problem
planSpec.stakes: the shop can rent gear only by cannibalizing its profitable new-equipment sales
planSpec.requiredBeat: Julien tags one camera as rental-only and shows how the old retailer would lose a sale every time it copied the move.

examples.scenario: At 6:42 p.m., Julien zips a rented lens into a padded case behind the used-camera counter. A red rental tag hangs from the camera body, and the new-equipment margin sheet is taped beside the deposit receipt. The retailer two blocks away can copy the service by tomorrow, but each weekend rental may replace a full sale. Julien must decide whether the shop will protect its shelf or chase his model.
examples.whatToDo: Price the rental around the customer job and trace the sale the retailer would sacrifice to copy it. The barrier is the lost new-equipment margin, not the rental tag.
examples.whyItMatters: A visible model is not automatically easy to imitate. If copying teaches customers to stop buying the incumbent product, the old seller has a reason to delay.

examples.title: Anya asks which invoice shrinks

planSpec.domain: low-cost legal forms platform serving uncontested tenant filings
planSpec.audience: product lead deciding whether a narrow flat-fee model threatens traditional hourly billing
planSpec.stakes: copying would teach clients to stop paying for routine partner time
planSpec.requiredBeat: Anya asks which line of hourly work the firm would have to erase, then highlights the routine filings her platform removes.

examples.scenario: "Which invoice would they volunteer to shrink?" Anya asks, sliding an hourly bill across the table. Her filing checklist for uncontested tenant cases is open beside a flat-fee page. "This line," her cofounder says, tapping routine partner review. Anya highlights the filings her platform removes. Before launch pricing locks, she must choose whether the law firm can copy without teaching clients to reject that bill.
examples.whatToDo: Identify the old billable line your workflow makes unnecessary. Launch only if the flat-fee model improves the customer job and makes the firm protect the hourly structure.
examples.whyItMatters: The firm can see the workflow, but copying it attacks the meaning of its own invoice. That self-cannibalization is the barrier the entrant needs.

examples.title: Chidi pins the returned chair tags

planSpec.domain: modular furniture refurbisher offering buy-back credits
planSpec.audience: operator deciding whether circular inventory is superior and hard for new-furniture stores to copy
planSpec.stakes: the incumbent would have to devalue full-price new inventory to match the credit model
planSpec.requiredBeat: Chidi pins returned chair tags under the new-stock price list and traces where the incumbent would poison its own premium shelf.

examples.scenario: In a Manchester furniture showroom at 8:15 a.m., sawdust gathers under the returned chair legs before the store opens. Chidi pins buy-back credit slips below the new-stock price list and traces the week customers began trading modules instead of buying full sets. The premium retailer could copy the credit, but every returned chair would sit under a shelf of new inventory. In the postmortem, Chidi marks where the old model would poison its own display.
examples.whatToDo: Keep the buy-back model tied to modular value and show exactly where a full-price retailer would devalue its own shelf by matching the credit.
examples.whyItMatters: The refurbisher can welcome returned inventory because its model is built for it. The incumbent sees the same move as a threat to the new-product premium it depends on.

examples.title: Marco reveals the lost-fee column

planSpec.audience: marketplace founder deciding whether removing commission hurts incumbent agencies
planSpec.stakes: agencies can copy only by attacking the fee structure their staff depends on
planSpec.requiredBeat: Marco has you choose whether the incumbent copies the no-commission screen or protects the commission ledger, then reveals the lost-fee column.

examples.scenario: You can hear the opening band through the office wall while Marco waits beside a booking screen and an agency commission ledger. He asks you to pick what the agency copies: the no-commission artist payout or the old fee column. You choose the screen. Marco turns the ledger around and reveals the lost-fee column that pays the booking staff. Now he has to decide whether that pain is enough to slow imitation.
examples.whatToDo: Compare the entrant payout with the incumbent fee ledger. Treat the no-commission model as protected only if copying it breaks the agency economics that keep the old channel alive.
examples.whyItMatters: The better artist payout is visible to everyone. The strategic question is whether the incumbent can adopt it without cutting the revenue column its organization is built around.

examples.title: Rachel colors the dealer channel red

planSpec.domain: pay-per-use industrial washer service replacing equipment sales
planSpec.audience: manufacturer strategy lead evaluating a service entrant
planSpec.stakes: copying usage billing would slow the incumbent equipment sales cycle and anger dealers
planSpec.requiredBeat: Rachel draws the dealer channel in red and asks which relationship breaks if the manufacturer copies the entrant.

examples.scenario: Which customer wins if the old seller copies the new model? In a leasing firm service bay at 2:30 p.m., Rachel stands over a dealer agreement, a usage meter, and an equipment quote for industrial washers. She draws the dealer channel in red and labels the commission that depends on full equipment sales. Before the manufacturer responds to the pay-per-use entrant, Rachel has to decide which relationship breaks when the old seller bills by the wash instead of by the machine.
examples.whatToDo: Map the dealer relationship before copying the usage meter. The service model is counter-positioned only if it helps customers while forcing the manufacturer to injure its sales channel.
examples.whyItMatters: A usage model can be superior for customers, but the barrier comes from the dealer conflict it creates for the incumbent. Without that conflict, imitation is easier.

questions.prompt: A meal-delivery startup sells prepaid workplace lunches. Established restaurants could sell the same plans, but doing so would train office workers away from full-price lunch orders. What makes this counter-positioning?
choices: The startup has a newer app than the restaurants.
The startup model is better for the customer and painful for restaurants to copy without hurting current sales.
The restaurants have more locations, so the startup must be protected.
questions.explanation: The entrant has a model that fits prepaid workplace demand, while incumbents would damage full-price lunches by copying it. The app and restaurant count are not the protective mechanism.

questions.prompt: A gym offers unlimited off-peak access for one flat monthly fee. Big gyms can copy the offer, but their profitable personal-training bundles depend on scarcity and scheduled visits. What should the entrant examine?
choices: Whether the flat fee wounds the incumbent bundle enough to delay imitation
Whether the big gyms have nicer equipment
Whether the entrant can describe the offer as disruptive
questions.explanation: The key is incumbent harm: copying the flat fee may weaken a profitable bundle. Equipment quality and disruptive language do not show why the old leader would hesitate.

questions.prompt: A direct-to-farmer seed seller cuts out regional dealers. The incumbent manufacturer can sell direct online, but dealers drive most current sales and would revolt. Which choice best reads the barrier?
choices: The barrier is the incumbent dealer conflict created by copying the direct model.
The barrier is that online selling is impossible for large firms.
The barrier is that farmers never buy from incumbents twice.
questions.explanation: The direct model threatens the incumbent channel that still produces revenue. Large firms can sell online, and nothing says farmers reject incumbents; the pain sits in the dealer relationship.

questions.prompt: A new insurer offers instant micro-policies for one-day events. Large insurers can copy the interface without changing pricing, sales channels, or underwriting. What does that imply?
choices: The entrant is automatically counter-positioned because it is simpler.
The large insurers will always refuse to copy anything new.
Counter-positioning is weak unless the new model damages the incumbent when copied.
questions.explanation: A better interface alone is not enough. If incumbents can copy without real damage to economics or channels, the barrier is thin. Simplicity may help customers but may not protect the entrant.

questions.prompt: A used-equipment rental service competes with retailers that earn high margins selling new machines. Customers prefer renting for short projects. Which sign would most strengthen the entrant case?
choices: Retailers have attractive showrooms.
Every rental the retailer offers would replace a profitable sale it wants to protect.
The rental service has a clever name.
questions.explanation: The rental model becomes hard to copy when it cannibalizes the incumbent sale. Showrooms and naming may affect perception, but they do not create the painful tradeoff.

questions.prompt: A clinic chain considers matching a mobile subscription competitor. The finance team shows subscriptions would fill slow mornings but reduce profitable individual visits. What is the incumbent trap?
choices: The chain lacks technology.
The competitor is new, so the chain cannot learn from it.
Copying helps in one area while injuring the revenue model the chain still relies on.
questions.explanation: The chain sees the move clearly, but adoption would harm profitable visits. That painful choice is the counter-positioning barrier; the issue is not ignorance or age.

questions.prompt: A flat-fee tax filing tool targets very simple returns. Accounting firms could build the same tool, but simple returns feed junior staff training and client upsells. What should the tool founder do?
choices: Emphasize the simple-return niche and the firm economics that make copying unattractive.
Avoid the niche because accounting firms are larger.
Copy the accounting firm website so customers feel familiar.
questions.explanation: The simple niche works if it helps customers and threatens a function firms still value. Size alone does not settle the contest, and copying the website misses the business-model conflict.

questions.prompt: A new publication gives all articles away free and sells data services to sponsors. Old newspapers can copy the free articles but would weaken subscriptions that still fund the newsroom. Which phrase names the issue?
choices: Learning economies
Self-cannibalization or analogous harm to the current model
Procedural switching costs
questions.explanation: The old newspaper may hesitate because free articles would damage subscription revenue. Learning economies involve cost improvement with repetition; switching costs involve customer migration pain.

questions.prompt: A startup leases high-end coffee machines by the cup. A manufacturer can match the usage meter, but dealers earn commissions on full machine sales. Which fact would weaken the counter-positioning claim?
choices: Dealers are important to the manufacturer today.
Customers like paying only when cups are brewed.
The manufacturer already sells mostly direct and dealers account for almost no revenue.
questions.explanation: If the threatened channel is no longer important, copying may not hurt much. Dealer dependence strengthens the barrier; customer preference shows the entrant benefit but not incumbent pain.

reviewCards.front: A newcomer has a cheaper model. What must you retrieve before calling it counter-positioned?
reviewCards.back: Retrieve the specific incumbent profit line, channel, or habit that copying would damage. A better model without incumbent pain is easier to imitate.

reviewCards.front: Why might an incumbent see the entrant clearly and still wait?
reviewCards.back: Because copying may injure the business that still pays the bills. The incumbent can be rationally hesitant when both copying and ignoring are painful.

reviewCards.front: A startup is new, digital, and cheaper. Why is that not enough?
reviewCards.back: Those traits describe difference, not protection. Counter-positioning requires a superior business model plus anticipated damage to the incumbent if it mimics the model.

reviewCards.front: What does the Scylla and Charybdis image help you remember?
reviewCards.back: The incumbent is caught between two bad options: copy and hurt the old model, or refuse and let the entrant grow. The trap is the source of hesitation.
It weakens when the incumbent can copy without serious cannibalization, channel conflict, customer re-education, or damage to the current economics.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Use counter-positioning as an incumbent-pain test. Do not stop at how the entrant is different; identify exactly what the incumbent would have to damage in order to copy.

ifThenPlans.plan: If I describe a model as disruptive, then I will write the incumbent profit line or channel it would cannibalize before I trust the claim.
If a rival can copy my offer, then I will ask whether copying helps or harms the business they are still protecting.
If I move from per-use to subscription or subscription to per-use, then I will map which incumbent customer habit the new price teaches against.
If my model bypasses a channel, then I will name the dealer, agent, or partner relationship an incumbent would anger by matching me.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Pick one entrant you admire. In three lines, write the superior model, the incumbent asset it threatens, and the sentence the incumbent would say to avoid copying it.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: For one week, collect three business models that look novel. For each, decide whether the novelty creates incumbent self-harm or merely gives customers another option.

memorableLines.text: The newcomer needs a better model, and the old leader needs a reason to flinch.
memorableLines.why: It compresses the benefit and barrier test into one concrete sentence.

memorableLines.text: The incumbent may see the move clearly and still delay because both choices hurt.
memorableLines.why: It captures the rational hesitation behind counter-positioning.

memorableLines.text: A strong entrant turns the old leader's strengths into hesitation.
memorableLines.why: It makes the incumbent trap memorable without generic disruption language.
